items.prompt: Which scenario most directly requires a state dp(i, j)?
constraints: The goal is to model the unresolved problem without compression.

options.text: A solver compares suffix a[i:] with suffix b[j:], and either index may advance independently.
A solver processes one suffix s[i:] and no other history affects future choices.
A solver computes a fixed formula for each i using only the previous scalar result.

feedback.reason: Independent movement through two suffixes creates distinct subproblems for each reachable pair (i, j).

blocks.text: A state coordinate is needed for each variable that can change independently and alter the future. In alignment, a transition may advance i, j, or both, so one coordinate cannot reconstruct the other. A one-suffix recurrence lacks that second axis. Overlap may occur among pairs, but the two-dimensional model comes from state sufficiency rather than from overlap alone.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.single_suffix: A single independently varying suffix boundary is naturally one-dimensional.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.fixed_window: The described future state has one progress coordinate and one live aggregate, not two independent subproblem axes.

items.prompt: Why cannot dp(i) replace dp(i, j) in a two-string alignment recurrence?
constraints: j is not determined by i.
Different j values expose different suffixes of the second string.

options.text: Any problem with two arrays must use exactly two DP dimensions.
A one-dimensional table is always slower than a two-dimensional table.
The same i can be paired with different j values whose remaining matches and optimal alignment lengths differ.

feedback.reason: Omitting j merges distinct second-string suffixes under one cache or table entry.

blocks.text: For a fixed i, one state may compare a[i:] with b[2:] and another with b[7:]. Their legal matches and result can differ, so they are not future-equivalent. The need for two dimensions follows from independent progress, not simply from having two arrays. A later rolling-row optimization can reduce physical storage while retaining the logical pair.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_arrays_rule: Two inputs do not mechanically imply two dimensions; dimensions follow independent future-relevant state variables.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.memory_speed: The failure is semantic state collision, not a universal performance relationship.

items.prompt: A grid recurrence reaches every one of R × C cells and does O(1) work per cell. Which comparison is accurate?
constraints: Both implementations use correct identical state and transition semantics.

options.text: Tabulation examines all paths explicitly and is exponential.
Memoization and tabulation both take O(RC) time; constants, stack depth, and locality determine practical differences.
Memoization takes O(R + C) because it follows paths rather than cells.

feedback.reason: Dense reachability makes the number of distinct computed states Θ(RC) for both evaluation strategies.

blocks.text: Memoization collapses repeated path prefixes into one result per cell, while tabulation writes each cell once. Both therefore perform Θ(RC) constant-time transitions. Top-down may use recursion and hash or table lookup; bottom-up can use contiguous loops and known boundaries. The two-dimensional state model does not privilege memoization by itself.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.memo_linear: Although each path has that length, the memoized solver still evaluates every distinct reachable cell once.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.tab_exponential: Tabulation aggregates path counts per cell rather than enumerating complete paths.

items.prompt: Order the construction of a prefix-based two-string DP table.
constraints: Interior cell (i, j) reads smaller-coordinate neighbors.
The answer is at (m, n).

elements.text: Initialize the empty-prefix row and column.
Fill cells with increasing i and j so all predecessor cells are ready.

feedback.reason: The empty-prefix boundaries are dependencies of the first interior cells and must be established before row-major filling.

blocks.text: Boundary prefixes seed every interior dependency

items: Allocate coordinates 0..m and 0..n so empty-prefix states exist alongside all nonempty prefixes.
Initialize the first row and first column from the recurrence’s empty-prefix semantics.
Fill the interior with increasing i and j so above, left and diagonal-up-left predecessors are already final.
Read dp[m][n] only after it represents both complete input prefixes.

blocks.text: The boundary row and column are semantic subproblems, not padding. Filling the interior before them would propagate defaults; reading the terminal coordinate early would return a partial result.

blocks.title: 2D construction
blocks.text: Allocate boundaries → initialize empty prefixes → fill dependency-safe interior → read dp[m][n].

items.prompt: When is replacing a full m × n table with previous/current rows justified?
constraints: Rows are evaluated in increasing order.
The output contract is known.

options.text: Every transition reads only the current and immediately previous row, and no later consumer needs older rows.
Whenever the logical state has two coordinates.
Whenever the final optimum value appears in the last row.

feedback.reason: Compression follows row liveness and output requirements, not the mere existence of a two-dimensional state.

blocks.text: If no transition ever reads beyond the previous row, older rows become dead after the next row is complete. They may be discarded when the final output also does not need them for tracing or queries. One-row compression requires an additional proof about in-place old and new versions. A recurrence with longer-range rows or full-table reconstruction breaks this boundary.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_two_d: Logical dimensionality alone does not limit dependency distance or reconstruction needs.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_values_somewhere: The final location does not prove that intermediate updates can be computed without older rows.

items.prompt: dp(i, j) is the minimum insertions and deletions needed to transform prefix a[:i] into b[:j]. Which boundary initialization is correct?
constraints: Replacing a character is not an allowed single operation.
Inserting or deleting one character costs 1.

options.text: Set the whole first row and first column to 0 because one prefix is empty.
Set every non-origin boundary cell to 1 because only one side is empty.
dp(i, 0) = i and dp(0, j) = j.

feedback.reason: Converting to empty deletes every source character, while converting from empty inserts every target character.

blocks.text: Boundary states are complete subproblems, not generic padding. dp(i, 0) needs i deletions and dp(0, j) needs j insertions; the origin is zero. These values seed the interior recurrence and encode the permitted operation costs. Uniform zero or one defaults would make longer empty-prefix transformations artificially cheap.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_zero: Transforming a nonempty prefix to or from empty requires one deletion or insertion per character.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_one: The cost grows with the nonempty prefix length, not merely with the fact that it is nonempty.

items.prompt: A grid solver tracks position (r, c) and may remove up to k blocked cells. Is dp(r, c) sufficient?
constraints: The number of removals remaining changes which future cells can be entered.
Different paths can reach the same cell with different remaining removals.

options.text: Yes. Because paths overlap at a cell, their resource histories can be merged.
No. The state must also distinguish remaining removals, such as dp(r, c, remaining).
Yes. A grid is two-dimensional, so row and column always define the DP state.

feedback.reason: The same cell with different remaining removals has a different set of legal continuations.

blocks.text: Row and column identify location but not the solver's remaining capability. A path arriving with one removal left can cross a future obstacle that a path with zero cannot, so those states are not future-equivalent. The logical state is therefore augmented beyond two coordinates. This illustrates that '2D DP' describes a state model, not simply a 2D input layout.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.position_enough: Geometric dimension does not capture an independent resource that changes future choices.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.overlap_removes_resource: Overlap permits merging only when complete future-relevant state components, including remaining removals, are equal.

items.prompt: A grid path answer depends on row, column, and how many obstacle removals remain. Which state model is sufficient?

options.text: dp(r, c, remainingRemovals), because all three coordinates can affect future legal paths.
dp(r, c), because the remaining removal budget can be inferred from location.
dp(k), because every cell has the same movement options.
Store every previous cell sequence even though only position and remaining budget affect future moves.

feedback.reason: An independent resource remaining at the same location creates a third future-relevant state coordinate.

blocks.text: Two paths can reach the same cell with different remaining removal budgets and therefore different future feasibility. The full path history is unnecessary if no other future rule depends on it. Dimensionality follows state sufficiency, not the visual number of input arrays.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.row_col_only: The same cell with different remaining budgets can have different answers.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.budget_only: Position determines which neighbors and obstacles remain available.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.full_path_history: History beyond the retained future-relevant coordinates creates redundant states.

items.prompt: A recurrence for cell (r,c) reads (r-1,c), (r,c-1), and (r-1,c-1). What does that imply about a one-row compression?

options.text: A one-row implementation needs a temporary old-diagonal value and an order that preserves up, left, and diagonal semantics.
Only the left value is needed because all grid recurrences can be read from one row.
Always scan columns right to left so every predecessor remains old.
Delete the previous row before processing because the current row contains all needed cells.

feedback.reason: The diagonal predecessor is overwritten when the current row reuses the column slot, so it needs explicit liveness handling.

blocks.text: At c, the old slot provides up; the updated c-1 provides left; and the old c-1 is the diagonal. A temporary variable carries that old c-1 before it is replaced. The scan direction depends on the recurrence, and blindly deleting the previous row loses up values.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.left_only: The recurrence explicitly reads a value from the previous row and the diagonal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reverse_columns_always: Direction must preserve the particular dependency set; reverse is not universally safe.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.delete_previous_row: The previous row supplies live up and diagonal predecessors.

items.prompt: A grid DP has R×C possible cells but obstacles make only K cells reachable. Which modeling choice should be considered?

options.text: Compare dense tabulation O(RC) with sparse memoization or frontier storage O(K), including access overhead and output needs.
Use a full table because a two-dimensional state can never be sparse.
Use a map because every obstacle guarantees that sparse storage is faster.
Compute all cells and treat obstacles as presentation-only metadata.

feedback.reason: The logical state space and the reachable state set can have different sizes, so storage strategy is workload- and representation-dependent.

blocks.text: Bottom-up dense tables give predictable locality when most cells are reached. Top-down memoization or a sparse frontier can avoid unreachable cells when K is small, but map overhead and transition access matter. Obstacles remain part of state legality in either representation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dense_always: Dense storage is not the only representation when many states are unreachable.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sparse_always: Sparse maps have overhead and may lose to dense arrays when the grid is mostly reachable.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_obstacles: A path through a blocked cell violates the problem's transition contract.

items.prompt: What does (i,j) usually represent in pairwise sequence DP?
constraints: The stated DP contract applies.
State dependencies must remain valid.

options.text: A subproblem for the first i elements of one sequence and first j of the other.
Arbitrary storage coordinates with no input meaning.
Only i matters; j is spare storage.
Every cell represents both full inputs.

feedback.reason: The accepted option preserves the DP state contract.

blocks.text: The state meaning, dependency order, and output contract must agree.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.storage: A DP coordinate must define a subproblem.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one: The second sequence changes the answer.

items.prompt: Why does sequence-alignment DP need a complete base row and column?
constraints: The stated DP contract applies.
State dependencies must remain valid.

options.text: They define aligning a nonempty prefix against an empty one and anchor the table.
The origin is enough.
Both boundaries are always zero.
Reject empty sequences.

feedback.reason: The accepted option preserves the DP state contract.

blocks.text: The state meaning, dependency order, and output contract must agree.

constraints: The stated DP contract applies.
State dependencies must remain valid.

options.text: Consume one side, the other side, or both, then combine alternatives by the objective.
They are redundant copies of one state.
Always take the maximum.
Read (i+1,j+1) in bottom-up order.

feedback.reason: The accepted option preserves the DP state contract.

blocks.text: The state meaning, dependency order, and output contract must agree.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicates: Changing either coordinate changes the subproblem.

items.prompt: When can a 2D DP table be reduced to O(n) space?
constraints: The stated DP contract applies.
State dependencies must remain valid.

options.text: After proving row dependencies and update order, use rolling rows and retain provenance if a path is required.
Every 2D DP needs one scalar.
Overwrite in any order.
A compressed table always reconstructs the same path.

feedback.reason: The accepted option preserves the DP state contract.

blocks.text: The state meaning, dependency order, and output contract must agree.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.scalar: Many transitions need a prior row.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.any: Writes can destroy left or diagonal reads.
